coverage.category: 1. Household employers: domestic workers, live-in carers, nannies
coverage.found: 28,791 foreign domestic workers in Q1 2026 (LAB figure quoted in al.gov.mo reply). June and Aug 2026 lawmaker questions ask for regulation of intermediaries, cross-department data sharing, and proof of repatriation (Law on Hiring Non-Resident Workers art. 26). These are proposals, not enacted law. Nothing new beyond K02.

coverage.category: 2. Scrap-metal dealers
coverage.found: One Chinese-language search found no Macau-specific scrap/second-hand register source (results were other jurisdictions). Unverified, not confirmed as a Macau duty.

coverage.category: 3. Second-hand dealers and pawnbrokers
coverage.found: No Macau register source found. Pawnshops are DNFBPs: they must report transactions of MOP 500,000 or more to GIF (secondary press summary). See C07.

coverage.category: 4. Gold and jewellery buyers
coverage.found: Jewellers are DNFBPs under the existing AML regime. Gold/platinum marking law is K06 (rejected). Draft AML overhaul in sector consultation mid-2026. See C07.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No search spent; budget used on higher-yield categories.

coverage.category: 6. Livestock traders, markets and animal transport
coverage.found: Urban microstate with no meaningful livestock trade (judgement, not searched). Animal-trade establishments are covered under category 9 and C03.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: No search spent. Slaughter is run by the municipal bureau (IAM) (not verified).

coverage.category: 8. Beekeepers
coverage.found: No beekeeping sector in a 33 km2 urban territory (judgement, not searched).

coverage.category: 9. Veterinary practices and veterinary medicine sellers
coverage.found: The Animal Clinical Veterinary Services and Commercial Activities law took effect 1 Apr 2024. Four types of establishment (vet, breeding, sale, boarding) are covered. Provisional licences valid 1 Apr 2025 to 31 Mar 2027. IAM issued 25 vet-clinic and 59 animal-business provisional licences. The gov.mo notice describes no record-keeping or periodic reporting beyond displaying the licence. See C03.

coverage.category: 10. Well drillers and water abstraction
coverage.found: No groundwater abstraction sector in Macau (judgement, not searched).

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: No search spent.

coverage.category: 12. Lift, boiler and pressure-equipment owners and inspectors
coverage.found: Law 14/2022 on lifts has been in force since 1 Apr 2024: registration with DSSOPT, a maintenance contract and a separate inspection entity, at least one inspection a year. About 10,500 lifts, 39 maintenance entities, 7 inspection entities. Admin Reg 39/2023 sets the technical rules and also covers car lifts. Nothing new beyond K01.

coverage.category: 13. Small water systems
coverage.found: Single concessionaire supplies water (judgement, not searched).

coverage.category: 14. Pesticide and fertiliser dealers and applicators
coverage.found: Negligible agriculture (judgement, not searched).

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: No dedicated search. Only the domestic-helper intermediary angle was seen, under category 1.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: No search spent.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: No search spent.

coverage.category: 18. Transport operators: minibus, taxi, moto-taxi, small trucking and bus fleets
coverage.found: DSAT is amending Law 3/2019 (light taxis) to allow e-hailing taxis, consultation Dec 2025 to early 2026. 800 more taxis are planned for 2026. Uber returned as metered taxi in Feb 2026. Two extra general licences were issued in Sep 2025, up to 50 vehicles each. Few licence holders, so the buyer group is small. Tour-bus rules were not found. See C05.

coverage.category: 19. Market traders, street vendors, money changers
coverage.found: Money-changer AML is K09. No other finding.

coverage.category: 20. Small licensed premises with inspections: tattoo studios, driving schools, childminders and nurseries, small food producers, hunting outfitters
coverage.found: Supplementary teaching and childcare-custody centres have had their own law and rules since 1 May 2023. DSEDJ has made over 2,500 inspections, vets staff qualifications, and requires centres serving meals to report to it. A draft law for private further-education centres reached the Legislative Assembly in June 2026. Childcare nurseries are still governed by scattered instruments. See C04.

coverage.category: 21. Fuel stations and fuel or LPG distributors
coverage.found: Licensing rests on Decree-Law 20/89/M. About 22 fuel stations and 20+ LPG distributors. 2026 news covers a diesel subsidy (11 May to 10 Jul 2026) and planned new stations, but no new reporting duty found. Small buyer group. Nothing new.

coverage.category: 22. Grain, coffee, cocoa and other commodity traders, millers and warehouses
coverage.found: No commodity trading or milling sector (judgement, not searched).

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: No search spent.

coverage.category: 24. Private clinics, labs and other health providers that bill insurers or state schemes
coverage.found: The Health Bureau's electronic health-voucher system settles claims monthly and uses big-data monitoring and spot checks (MOP 700 per resident in 2025, about MOP 520m budget in 2026). The government has consulted (Apr 2025) on replacing Decree-Laws 22/99/M and 84/90/M with a unified private medical institutions law, adding day hospitals. No enactment found. See C06.

coverage.category: 25. Pharmacies, medicine importers, and users of controlled chemicals or precursors
coverage.found: Only partly covered by the health search. Nothing found on pharmacies. Not fully checked.

coverage.category: 26. Security, cleaning and manpower agencies, and the firms that hire their workers
coverage.found: Private security is under Law 4/2007, with a government PDF list of licensed firms. No 2025-26 amendment found. Cleaning and manpower agencies were not searched.

coverage.category: 27. Construction, mining and quarry contractors and suppliers: site registers, accreditation, local-content reports
coverage.found: The Urban Building Law 14/2021 was amended by Law 6/2026 (published 11 May 2026, in force in stages from 1 Jun 2026). It exempts low-risk works from licences, adds an e-platform for non-residential units under 120 m2, and adds penalties for false information. The first search returned only Dubai results. Contractor registration and site-register duties were not found. See C08.

coverage.category: 28. Notaries, land agents, real estate brokers and other professionals with periodic or anti-money-laundering reports
coverage.found: Real estate agents are licensed (3-year licence) and are DNFBPs under the AML regime (reporting at MOP 500,000 or more). A draft AML overhaul replacing the 2006 regime was in sector consultation in mid-2026 and would add a central beneficial-ownership register, phased in later. Notaries were not specifically covered. See C07.

coverage.category: 29. Hotels, guest houses and short-term rentals: guest registers, tourism levies
coverage.found: Hotel operators must pass guest data (guests aged 16 or older without local ID) to the security forces under a regulation effective 16 Nov 2022 (Macau Business). Short-term rentals are illegal under Law 3/2010 as amended by Law 3/2022: no lawful homestay category, fines MOP 200,000 to 800,000 per unit, 75 units sealed Jan to Apr 2026. See C09.

coverage.category: 30. Small exporters and importers facing traceability or certification rules: food, fish, timber, forest-risk commodities
coverage.found: IAM opened 25 cases in Jan to Jul 2026 over unquarantined ingredients, after inspecting over 5,800 premises, and urged operators to keep supplier quarantine papers and import permits. Food Safety Law offences carry up to 5 years' prison or fines of MOP 50,000 to 600,000 (press summary). The page was blocked (403), so only the search snippet was read. See C02.

coverage.category: 31. Building management and owners' corporations (Law 14/2017, Law 12/2017 management-company licensing)
coverage.found: Management bodies must publish annual accounts at owners' meetings (Law 14/2017 arts 22 and 25, per a court ruling). Management companies need a Housing Bureau licence valid 3 years, renewable. Owners must give a copy of meeting minutes to the Housing Bureau. See C01.

coverage.category: 32. Fire-safety duty holders under Law 15/2021 (buildings and premises)
coverage.found: Law 15/2021 puts fire-safety duties on owners, occupiers, building management bodies and 'qualified commercial business owners'. Security Secretary replies in 2025-26 say systems must be inspected and maintained regularly. The exact certificate, who may inspect, and the deadline were not found. See C01.

coverage.category: 33. Urban Building Law periodic maintenance cycle (Law 14/2021)
coverage.found: A 2022 reply says buildings must be maintained at 10 years of use and every 5 years after; non-compliance can bring utility cut-off and owner fines of MOP 2,500 to 50,000. Whether Law 6/2026 changed this was not confirmed. See C01 and C08.

coverage.category: 34. Animal establishments licensing (vet, breeding, sale, boarding)
coverage.found: See category 9 and C03.

coverage.category: 35. Supplementary teaching, childcare-custody and further-education centres
coverage.found: See category 20 and C04.

coverage.category: 36. Taxi and e-hailing regime (Law 3/2019 amendment)
coverage.found: See category 18 and C05.

coverage.category: 37. Private medical institutions law reform and health-voucher scheme
coverage.found: See category 24 and C06.

coverage.category: 38. AML regime overhaul for designated non-financial businesses
coverage.found: See categories 28 and 4, and C07.

coverage.category: 39. Illegal accommodation law (Law 3/2010 as amended by 3/2022)
coverage.found: See category 29 and C09.

coverage.category: 5. Used car parts and vehicle dismantlers
coverage.found: No dismantler licensing regime found. A 2021 Legislative Assembly (al.gov.mo) interpellation says about 5,000 end-of-life vehicles a year and that government and private car yards are near saturation. Workshops (including dismantling) are still governed by Decree-Law 47/98/M, which only sets night-time limits; there is no licence. A replacement bill, 'Regime for Regulation of Specific Businesses', was on the 2025 legislative plan and is reported (Plataforma Media, July 2026, via search snippet; the fetch returned 403) to be in consultation. The consultation text reportedly covers about 129 workshops doing spraying, welding or lithium-battery assembly or dismantling, keeps administrative approval, and sets a 60-day temporary registration after entry into force plus one year to remedy or relocate. Not yet enacted; one-off, small number of firms. See the candidate on this.

coverage.category: 7. Small abattoirs and butchers
coverage.found: Nothing new. Slaughter is done by Macau Slaughterhouse Co. Ltd, in which the municipal bureau (IAM) holds 61.075% (Legislative Assembly reply). Retail meat stalls are licensed by IAM under the 1996 rules as amended by Administrative Regulations 17/2015 and 8/2016, which are premises and hygiene conditions with no recurring filing. Live animals come only from registered mainland farms, and checks are done by the state. No recurring duty falling on small butchers was found, so nothing for software.

coverage.category: 11. Septic, sanitation and waste haulers
coverage.found: No Macau licence or register for septic, grease-trap or used-cooking-oil haulers found in three searches; results were mostly Hong Kong (EPD waste cooking oil collector registration, which is not Macau law). A Legislative Assembly interpellation (2021/2022) says used cooking oil collection in Macau is a near gap with few private collectors. The recycling trade has DSPA pollution-control guidelines and an equipment and vehicle subsidy scheme (2026 reply). Nothing mandatory and recurring found. Not verified on DSPA's own site.

coverage.category: 15. Labour contractors and recruitment agencies
coverage.found: Employment agencies are licensed by DSAL under Law 16/2020 (Employment Agency Activity Law). Licence renewal is 45 to 90 days before expiry (MOP 10,000; branch MOP 5,000; fee doubled if late; about 30 days processing). Fee-charging agencies must lodge a MOP 300,000 bank guarantee and publish and send DSAL a fee list. Job-seeker fees are capped at 50% of the first month's salary. Agencies must supply practitioners' names and licence numbers, and advertisements must show the licence number. Licensed agencies numbered 134 in 2020 (outdated). Only two designated agencies handle mainland-Chinese domestic helpers. Agencies cannot place non-residents already in Macau (2026 interpellation). The earlier 2018 bill coverage (macaubusiness) is superseded by Law 16/2020. No agency-specific software found (see candidate). The agencies are the same buyer as K02.

coverage.category: 16. Cemeteries, burial societies and funeral services
coverage.found: Public cemeteries and tombs are run by IAM. Administrative Regulation 12/2025 (Official Gazette, 13 Oct 2025) amends cemetery Regulation 37/2003; the text could not be fetched (host not reachable), so changes are unknown. Funeral services have no licensing regime found. A May 2024 interpellation says one company handles body transfers and funeral fees are opaque, and the Civil Registry plans a funeral-affairs website. Cremation is done on the mainland. Burial licences and 7-year tomb rights are IAM processes. No recurring register or return duty on private funeral firms found; nothing for software.

coverage.category: 17. Community and religious bodies: associations, charities, halal and kosher supervision
coverage.found: Associations are governed by Law 2/99/M (right of association) and the Civil Code. A government draft law to replace both went to 45-day public consultation from 17 Aug 2026 to 23 Sept 2026 (macaubusiness). The registry is run by DSI, which becomes sole supervisor. About 12,400 registered groups, about 60% active; the draft adds a dormancy mechanism, minimum 7 founders, stricter bylaws and names, and dissolution powers (including national security). No financial-reporting duty was confirmed in the draft. Law 2/99/M art. 19 requires publishing accounts for groups receiving public subsidies above a threshold. The Trade Union Law lets associations convert to unions between 1 Jan 2025 and 31 Dec 2027 (a few groups only). No halal or kosher supervision regime found. Candidate listed.

coverage.category: 23. Co-operatives, credit unions and savings groups
coverage.found: One search found nothing on Macau co-operatives (results were Taiwan law, AMCM fee orders and gaming credit law). From memory only and unverified: co-operatives sit under Decree-Law 52/99/M and are registered by DSE. No credit unions or savings groups found. No evidence of a recurring return duty or a sizeable buyer group. Unchecked: DSE co-operative register and count.

result.competitor: No Macau compliance-calendar product was found for the 10/5-year cycle, accounts deadlines or licence renewal. Nearby local apps: 澳物通 (Macau, Gaudisheng Tech; fee payment, repairs, complaints), Ulive (Hengqin Yun Ting; notices, fee bills, payment, repairs) and e管家/ec.Life (links owners, managers and owners' management bodies; notices, incident reports). Any of them could add reminders. Government help comes through the Building Maintenance Fund subsidies, and no state calendar tool was found.
result.duty: Real, but mostly triggered by events rather than filed on a schedule. Law 14/2021 Art. 15(1) says maintenance is required "when needed": 10 years after the use licence, then every 5 years. Under Art. 15(7) the management body does the work on common parts in buildings with multiple owners. Under Art. 15(2) DSSCU can demand a technician's condition report only when it finds signs of poor upkeep. Fines under Art. 42: MOP 2,500–50,000 for individuals and 5,000–100,000 for legal persons for not submitting the report; MOP 5,000–200,000 for individuals and 15,000–500,000 for legal persons for not completing the works. A 2022 AL question says water and power can be cut off. Law 6/2026 (gazetted 11 May 2026, phased in from 1 June 2026) amended Arts. 4, 5, 7, 19–21, 25, 28, 42, 54, 57 and 58. Art. 15 shows no amendment marker on Wikisource, but the exact new Art. 42 amounts were not reached because the PDF could not be read. Law 14/2017 requires annual accounts to be reported and lets owners see documents (Art. 43). A court case (TSI 574/2021) confirms there are disputes over accounts. Under Law 12/2017 the IH licence lasts 3 years, can be renewed, and needs a technical director. The fire-safety mechanics of Law 15/2021 were not checked.
result.market: Not found. Searches found no IH count of licensed building management companies or registered owners' management bodies. The licence regime is confirmed, but the number of licensees is unverified. Macau is small, so the number of licensed firms is probably limited (an inference, not checked). Owners' bodies in older buildings are often volunteers and are unlikely to pay.
result.reason: The duties are real and in force, but they are soft and the market is small. Under Law 14/2021 Art. 15, maintenance at 10 years and then every 5 years is required "when needed". The building management body handles common parts. DSSCU asks for a condition report only when it sees signs of poor upkeep, so nothing is filed on a schedule. Fines are MOP 2,500–50,000 for individuals and up to 100,000 for companies. Law 6/2026 amended Art. 42 penalties but appears to leave Art. 15 alone. Law 14/2017 requires annual accounts and owner access, and IH management licences last 3 years. No Macau compliance-calendar tool was found. Local apps (澳物通, Ulive, e管家) cover fees, notices and repairs and could add this. The licensee count was not found. Buyers are few and mostly unpaid volunteers.

Duty is real but thin. Law 5/2013 art. 5 requires food operators to keep incoming and outgoing records or documents "within a specified period"; no retention length or form is stated, and no penalty is tied to record-keeping alone. The MOP 50,000-600,000 fines and prison terms apply to unsafe or unquarantined food. IAM's Aug 2026 enforcement (25 cases, 5,800+ inspections) is a nudge, not a mandated log or e-filing. Nothing found that already does this job, but searches were limited and the market size was not found. Weak pain, no fixed frequency, no filing deadline, and a paper-habit buyer base with low willingness to pay. The IAM article itself was not opened.

result.reason: The duty looks real. Press reports say pawnshops, jewellers, real estate agents and auction houses must report transactions of MOP 500,000 or more, and the 2006 AML law (Law 2/2006) is being replaced by a draft in departmental consultation. I could not open the law or GIF guidance, so frequency, penalty and in-force status are unconfirmed. I found no local AML software aimed at these sectors, but my searches were thin. The market is small: GIF's H1 2026 data puts "other" reporters at 7.6% of reports, and I found no firm counts. The reporting is event-driven rather than a recurring filing, and the draft law is not yet in force. Notaries are not covered. Willingness to pay is likely low, so the kit is a weak niche.

The draft law is real. A 45-day consultation ran to 23 Sept 2026, covering about 12,400 registered associations. Roughly 40% have been inactive for at least five years. DSI would be the sole supervisor and would run a dormancy process: notify, then dissolve if there is no response. I found nothing on annual accounts, member-list filing, bylaw-conformity deadlines or a transition period. The bill is not enacted, so there is no recurring duty yet. Law 2/99/M art. 19 requires subsidised groups to publish accounts, but the government reportedly does not enforce it. The one-off dormancy/re-registration trigger is weak. Buyers are volunteer groups with low willingness to pay. I did not search for competitors beyond the claim's own search. Revisit if the bill adds annual filing.
